newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BUNDESBANK RATE OUTLOOK PROMTS FRESH EMU DEBATE.
newsitem.headline: BUNDESBANK RATE OUTLOOK PROMTS FRESH EMU DEBATE.

text.p: A possible rise in German interest rates, which some economists believe is needed to slow the mark's decline, has prompted debate over the effects such a move might have on Europe's planned single currency.

The Bundesbank hinted it may start to tighten the reins of monetary policy last week when it refused to specify where the rate for its key securities repurchase tender (repo) would be during late August.
A number of economists say the lack of clarity may open the door to a variable repo rate, which would effectively tighten credit conditions in Germany.
This may seem reasonable against the backdrop of the mark's sharp depreciation against the dollar, modest growth in Germany and a mixed economic picture across Europe.
But for European economic and monetary union (EMU), the implications of a change in the interest rate cycle of Europe's biggest economy are varied and somewhat difficult to gauge.

However, most analysts reckon the damage to the current high degree of convergence in European interest rates and currencies ahead of EMU's January 1999 launch would be limited. "I don't see this as a problem for EMU. Quite a number of countries would benefit given that short-term rates are above those in Germany," said one London-based economist.
In a newspaper interview published on Wednesday, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said the dilemma of the weak economy and mark must be handled with "extreme care."
Among the various points economists stressed in judging whether such a policy shift was possible, several stood out:

-- A somewhat tighter monetary policy may be necessary due to the inflationary consequences of the lower mark. What worries the Bundesbank most is the pace of the currency's decline. If the recent trend were to continue inflation could rise to between two and three percent within a year's time.

-- A slight rise in rates would have little effect on continued EMU convergence given that many countries already have short-term rates somewhat above those in Germany. Spain, Portugal and Ireland were cited as examples.
-- Tightening policy a bit now would also prevent the need for a much more aggressive interest rate rise later, one that could have harmful consequences to the single currency.

-- Others, however, said verbal intervention would be more effective than allowing short-rates to rise, particularly given that the mark's weakness reflected structural economic problems in Germany and expectations of a weak euro.

-- Unless the Bundesbank was prepared to tighten monetary policy aggressively, which was unlikely in the present economic situation, a repo rise could fuel the speculative fervor of markets to push the mark even lower.

-- One big uncertainty is France. Should the Banque de France fail to follow the Bundesbank's lead, the resulting currency turmoil on European markets might be considerable. And even if French rates were raised, there are doubts about how the new Socialist government would respond given that France's economy is still struggling compared with Germany and other countries.
"At the moment its fairly unlikely the Bundesbank would go straight to a variable repo," said Jan Hatzius, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
Worries over how such a decision would be greeted in financial markets was a major reason for caution at this point, he said.

Hatzius said the Bundesbank -- already tainted with the image of not being wholeheartedly in support of a broad-based and therefore "soft" euro -- would be careful not to reinforce such perceptions by raising rates too prematurely.
From an economic standpoint, others argued that a dollar/mark level of 1.80 to 1.90 should be tolerable, particularly as it would ensure a better pace of growth in Germany and throughout Europe.
The rate stood at around 1.84 on Wednesday.
Should the dollar accelerate beyond such a range, Europe's most powerful central bank might have little choice but to use the interest-rate lever.
"The question is at what point do they get concerned enough to move again," said Bruce Kasman, European economist at J.P. Morgan in London.

One other twist was the effect such a move would have on Italy's chances of qualifying for monetary union. While the lira would likely suffer a bit, most believed that Rome would not necessarily be forced to follow the Bundesbank to higher short-term rates.
($ = 0.931 European Currency Unit ECUs)
